articles.title: Shipping Industry Statement Calling for Convergence Towards Pragmatic Alternative Global Framework
articles.summary: As the International Maritime Organization prepares for MEPC 85, the industry calls on Member States to seize this opportunity to bridge differences surrounding the IMO Mid-Term Measures and converge toward an alternative global framework. articles.body: Shipping Industry Statement Calling for Convergence Towards Pragmatic Alternative Global Framework in International Shipping News 28/11/2026 As the International Maritime Organization prepares for MEPC 85, the industry calls on Member States to seize this opportunity to bridge differences surrounding the IMO Mid-Term Measures and converge toward an alternative global framework. The industry highlights preference for a globally aligned and effective regulatory framework over fragmented regional measures undermining a coherent approach for international shipping. Achieving this requires constructive engagement with the range of alternative proposals on the table, identifying areas of convergence and drawing on their most effective elements to develop a solution that balances strategic ambition with market and technological readiness. In this respect, we encourage Member States to constructively consider viable bridging solutions, including those that are responsive to market developments, under a trajectory reflective of shipping realities. Particularly under the current strained global context, heightened concerns around global energy security, food security and the affordability of essential goods further underscore the need for a framework that incentivizes all effective options for reducing emissions and improving energy efficiency, but most importantly avoiding disproportionate costs that ultimately drive inflation and burden end consumers globally. In that spirit, the industry expects that agreement on an effective global framework should provide a common regulatory basis for addressing the sector’s greenhouse gas emissions, removing the need for additional local or regional regulations. MEPC 85 and the resumed MEPC/ES.2 represent a crucial crossroads for international shipping. Pragmatism must prevail to prevent persisting divisions that led to adjournment a year prior, supporting the industry toward action constructively within current capacity and along with new solutions. A durable and effective framework must be grounded in the realities and context of global shipping, including the availability, scalability and affordability of alternative fuels, technologies and infrastructure. Any pathway that can deliver emissions reductions should be considered. These considerations are essential to ensuring that regulatory ambition translates into achievable requirements, supports investment and can be implemented across the diverse segments of the global fleet. To that end, it is important that any alternative global framework is subject to thorough consideration of its practical implications, supported by robust economic analysis and assessment of its impacts to the industry and the wider context it serves. articles.title: Newbuilding Activity: Orderbook At All Time High
articles.summary: Newbuilding ordering activity is booming and this is starting to be reflected on the numbers. In a recent report, shipbroker Banchero Costa, revealed that “the orderbook for bulkcarriers, crude, product and chemical tankers, LNG and LPG carriers and containerships reached 172.3 mln CGT at end-October 2026 (5,488...
articles.body: Newbuilding Activity: Orderbook At All Time High in Hellenic Shipping News 28/11/2026 N ewbuilding ordering activity is booming and this is starting to be reflected on the numbers. In a recent report, shipbroker Banchero Costa, revealed that “the orderbook for bulkcarriers, crude, product and chemical tankers, LNG and LPG carriers and containerships reached 172.3 mln CGT at end-October 2026 (5,488 ships), +24.0% y-o-y and the highest of all time, above the 2007-2008 peak of 131.6 mln CGT. Containerships are 37.1% of it. Relative to the fleet, the orderbook is largest for LPG carriers (40.8%), containerships (40.3%) and LNG carriers (38.7%), and has risen fastest for crude tankers, to 29.2% from 15.0%. For bulkcarriers and tankers combined it is 19.7%, the highest since 2011”. Meanwhile, “contracting reached 50.9 mln CGT in Jan-Oct 2026, +43.8% y-o-y, led by crude tankers, LNG and LPG carriers and bulkcarriers; containership ordering eased. The pace has slowed since a strong first quarter: 26.2 mln CGT in 1Q, 11.9 in 2Q and 10.3 in 3Q. China took 73.5% of the CGT ordered in Jan-Oct 2026 and holds 68.5% of the orderbook. South Korea still leads in LNG and LPG carriers; Japan’s share of orders fell to 3.3%. Hengli (Dalian) alone took 14.2% of this year’s orders. Deliveries were 31.0 mln CGT in Jan-Oct 2026 (+14.2% y-o-y). The contracted schedule rises to 52.0 mln CGT in 2027 and 61.3 mln CGT in 2028, against a previous high of 39.5 mln CGT in 2011. The delivery wave is heaviest for containerships, with 17.3% of the fleet scheduled for 2028, and crude tankers, with 12.0%. LPG and LNG carriers face 15.7% and 12.3% in 2027; bulkcarriers about 5% in each of 2027 and 2028. Capacity is stretched: Chinese yards are scheduled to deliver 65.2 mln DWT of bulkcarriers and tankers in 2027 and 92.7 mln DWT in 2028, against a record of 62.6 mln DWT in 2011. New and revived yards are due to deliver 16.5% of the 2028 total”, Banchero Costa said. Source: Banchero Costa The shipbroker added that “ead times have lengthened: ships ordered this year are due on average 33.6 months after contract, and 55.0% of this year’s orders (CGT) are due in 2029 or later. Demolition is minimal (2.6 mln DWT of bulkcarriers in Jan-Oct 2026), although 33% of the Aframax and 18% of the VLCC fleet is 20 years or older. Outlook: contracting to slow. With yards largely full until 2029 and prices high, we expect ordering to slow into 2027, especially for crude tankers”. Source: Banchero Costa Similarly, prices have remained stable at high levels. “Tanker and bulkcarrier prices should stay broadly stable (VLCC USD 131.0 mln, +6.9% y-o-y), and a 5-year-old VLCC at 153% of the newbuilding price keeps ordering attractive. ULCS and LNG carrier prices should stay softer as new Chinese capacity competes. Freight markets face the main risk in 2027-2028, especially for crude tankers and containerships, when today’s support from the Hormuz disruption and longer voyages may have eased. US port fees on Chinese-built ships could return; the US-China trade truce ends on 10 February 2027. Conclusion: yard capacity stays tight to the end of the decade and the 2027-2028 deliveries are already fixed. How heavy the wave proves depends on slippage, especially at new yards, and on demolition once earnings weaken”, the shipbroker said. During the past week, Banchero Costa reported that “newbuilding activity covered a broad range of sectors, with reported orders spanning bulk carriers, containerships, car carriers, dry cargo vessels, ferries and gas carriers. The car carrier segment was particularly notable, with Global Car Carriers adding further units to its growing PCTC orderbook. Japanese and Chinese yards also secured new container and bulk carrier orders, while the gas sector saw fresh commitments for both LNG and LPG/ammonia carriers. In the bulk carrier sector, Leon Shipping & Trading reportedly contracted a 84,000 dwt bulk carrier at Hengli Heavy Industries, China, with delivery scheduled for June 2029. Nomikos also reportedly placed an order for an 82,000 dwt bulk carrier at Oshima, Japan, for delivery in March 2030. The car carrier sector saw further activity from Global Car Carriers. The company reportedly contracted 2x PCTCs at Zhoushan Changhong International, with deliveries scheduled for October and December 2030. These are the first car carriers to be constructed by the Chinese yard, with the vessels designed by SDARI in Shanghai. The owner also reportedly contracted 2x 8,600-car PCTCs at China Merchants Weihai, with deliveries scheduled for June and December 2031. The vessels will feature LNG dual-fuel propulsion, comply with IMO NOx Tier III and EEDI Phase 3 requirements, and include an option to switch from LNG dual fuel to ammonia. In the container sector, Eastern Pacific Shipping reportedly contracted 4x 9,000 teu containerships at Imabari, Japan. Two vessels are scheduled for delivery in June 2030, with the remaining pair due in December 2031. The vessels will feature conventional fuel propulsion. Finally, activity in the gas sector included Thenamaris’ reported order for 2x 174,000 cu.m. LNG carriers at Hyundai, South Korea, with delivery scheduled for December 2030, priced at approximately USD 243.7 million each. Foresight Group also reportedly contracted a 90,000 cu.m. LPG/ammonia carrier at Hyundai, priced at approximately USD 117.5 million, with delivery scheduled for October 2029”, the shipbroker concluded. articles.title: How emission reduction and commercial outcomes go hand in hand
articles.summary: As maritime emissions regulation becomes increasingly complex, owners, operators and charterers face a growing challenge: understanding what carbon compliance means for their commercial decisions. With the FuelEU Maritime and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) regulations already influencing economics, and...
articles.body: How emission reduction and commercial outcomes go hand in hand in International Shipping News 28/11/2026 A s maritime emissions regulation becomes increasingly complex, owners, operators and charterers face a growing challenge: understanding what carbon compliance means for their commercial decisions. With the FuelEU Maritime and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) regulations already influencing economics, and further developments at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) still under discussion, the cost of emissions can no longer be treated as a separate consideration. Fuel choices, operational efficiency and contractual arrangements are all playing an increasingly important role in determining the profitability of a voyage. However, while the regulatory landscape presents challenges, it is also creating new commercial opportunities. Understanding the value of emissions savings, managing compliance surpluses and identifying opportunities to improve operational efficiency can help shipping companies turn decarbonisation into a business advantage. These were among some of the key themes explored during a recent Baltic Exchange Emissions and Efficiency Update webinar, featuring Maximilian Schroer, Co-founder of BetterSea, Haris Zografakis, Senior Consultant at Stephenson Harwood and Executive Chairman of Blue Visby Services, and Martin Crawford-Brunt, Emissions Lead at Baltic Exchange. A key distinction in the current regulatory landscape is the difference between EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime. As Schroer explained, companies must consider several questions when managing their FuelEU position, such as which fuel they choose, where should they consume it, how should they trade any resulting surplus, and who ultimately controls its value? Pooling vessels FuelEU pooling is an important part of this equation. It allows vessels that perform better than the required greenhouse gas intensity target to transfer their surplus compliance balance to vessels in deficit, helping them avoid penalties while potentially creating a revenue stream for surplus-generating vessels. However, the value of that surplus depends on the cost of generating it, which varies considerably depending on the fuel choice. During 2025, BioLNG was the largest seller of compliance surplus and effectively set the market price. Although LNG offered a relatively low cost of surplus generation, much of the available surplus was banked by owners rather than sold. By 2026, the picture had changed, with Bio100 becoming the cheapest source of surplus generation. BetterSea’s FuelEU index provides a daily reference price for compliance surplus, based on executed trades. The 2025 volume-weighted average was approximately €193 per tonne, but prices have since fallen, with the monthly average reaching around €120 in June and €84 in October. This reflects the potential commercial attractiveness of purchasing surplus rather than facing a compliance penalty. The changing market also highlights the importance of understanding who is responsible for pooling. This depends on the contractual relationship, including whether a vessel is operated by its owner or on time charter, and the length of the charter period. Operators may focus on optimising buying and selling decisions within the reporting period, while owners with longer-term interests may wish to consider banking surplus for future use. In either case, charter parties need to reflect realistic market values, with index-based pricing helping to provide greater transparency and reduce the potential for disputes. Waiting at anchorage Regulation is only one part of the decarbonisation equation. Improving operational efficiency can also deliver significant commercial benefits, often without requiring a change of fuel or substantial investment in new technology. Zografakis highlighted the inefficiency created when ships sail at speed, only to spend extended periods waiting at anchorage. This results in unnecessary fuel consumption, higher emissions and additional costs for both owners and charterers. He noted that the ideal solution to this is by combining operational optimisation with a benefit-sharing arrangement between the parties. By adjusting sailing speeds and coordinating vessel arrival times with berth availability, vessels can reduce fuel consumption and time spent waiting at anchorage. Under the model discussed, the charterer compensates the owner for the additional time spent at sea, while fuel savings are shared between the parties, typically on a 50/50 basis, although this can be negotiated. The approach aims to improve the financial position of both parties compared with a conventional voyage, with emissions reductions of approximately 10-18% as an additional benefit. The optimisation process accounts for vessel performance, contractual requirements, terminal schedules, berth availability and environmental conditions, including first-come, first-served port arrangements. Baltic’s reliable benchmarks The wider message is that emissions reductions and commercial performance do not have to be competing objectives. With the right contractual and operational arrangements, improved efficiency can create a financial benefit for both sides of a charter. Understanding these opportunities requires reliable benchmarks and practical tools to translate regulatory requirements into financial terms. This is where the Baltic Exchange’s free emissions calculators have an important role to play. Developed to help the market navigate the growing complexity of emissions regulation, the calculators allow users to compare the relative financial and environmental implications of different fuel and operational choices against Baltic standard ships and standard routes. The FuelEU Maritime calculator allows users to select a vessel type and adjust key variables, including vessel size, speed, fuel consumption, fuel type and fuel prices. The results provide a comparison against a Baltic benchmark vessel operating on conventional very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO), helping users understand the potential impact on voyage costs. The TCE calculator provides another practical commercial application, converting a lump-sum voyage calculation into a TCE figure that incorporates ETS and FuelEU impacts. The calculators are designed to provide relative comparisons rather than absolute compliance assessments for individual vessels. By using a consistent market benchmark, they give owners, operators and charterers a common starting point for understanding the financial implications of different decisions and negotiating the allocation of costs and benefits. Trusted reference points As the industry becomes increasingly data-driven, commercial parties are still somewhat reluctant to share granular operational or financial data. Despite this, even where calculations can be automated, the market still needs trusted reference points when negotiating freight rates, compliance costs and the value of emissions savings. Ultimately, maritime decarbonisation is moving beyond the initial ambition-setting phase. Regulation is creating direct financial consequences, while new approaches to pooling, fuel selection and operational efficiency are opening up commercial opportunities. For owners, operators and charterers, the challenge is to understand where these opportunities lie and how to incorporate them into everyday commercial decisions. Whether choosing the most cost-effective fuel, managing FuelEU surplus, reducing unnecessary fuel consumption or negotiating a fair allocation of compliance costs, access to reliable market information is increasingly important. takeaways: Fuel choices, operational efficiency and contractual arrangements are all playing an increasingly important role in determining the profitability of a voyage.
However, while the regulatory landscape presents challenges, it is also creating new commercial opportunities.

Understanding the value of emissions savings, managing compliance surpluses and identifying opportunities to improve operational efficiency can help shipping companies turn decarbonisation into a business advantage.

articles.title: Are North-South container alliances on the way?
articles.summary: Speculation that Maersk and Ocean Network Express (ONE) could establish a North-South container shipping alliance raises an interesting question: are we approaching a new phase in liner industry cooperation, one in which alliances extend beyond the traditional East-West trades? Vessel-sharing agreements (VSAs) are...
articles.body: Are North-South container alliances on the way? in International Shipping News 28/11/2026 S peculation that Maersk and Ocean Network Express (ONE) could establish a North-South container shipping alliance raises an interesting question: are we approaching a new phase in liner industry cooperation, one in which alliances extend beyond the traditional East-West trades? Vessel-sharing agreements (VSAs) are not new to North-South routes, but the more structured and longer-lasting alliance partnerships have until now been confined to the Asia-Europe, Transpacific and Transatlantic trades, expanding only recently to the Middle East in a few isolated cases. These East-West routes handle the largest and most concentrated cargo volumes, providing the critical mass needed to justify deploying increasingly large vessels. Sharing ships enables carriers to spread operating costs, improve vessel utilisation and offer more comprehensive weekly networks without each having to operate an entirely independent service. The economics differ on North-South routes. Trades connecting Asia, Europe and North America with Latin America, Africa and Oceania generally have smaller and more fragmented cargo flows. Vessel sizes are consequently more varied, while port infrastructure, cargo imbalances and operational requirements can make network coordination more complicated. Historically, cooperation has therefore tended to take the form of individual VSAs, slot exchanges and regional consortia rather than extensive alliance structures. However, the strategic incentives for greater cooperation on North-South trades are becoming increasingly compelling. The average size of containerships deployed on these routes is rapidly increasing (see Table 2) due to the cascading effect from East-West trades, and with the industry facing substantial newbuilding deliveries over the next few years that trend is only going to continue. Therefore, pooling capacity and rationalising overlapping North-South services could offer considerable efficiencies for carriers, particularly on routes where maintaining multiple competing networks is difficult to justify. At present, this is all speculation with neither Maersk or ONE willing to comment. Ultimately, the significance would depend on the scope of any agreement, if one is reached at all. A collection of individual VSAs would represent an incremental development, whereas coordinated network planning across multiple North-South trades could mark a more fundamental shift in industry structure. If a broad alliance does indeed materialise and delivers meaningful cost and service advantages, it could encourage other carriers to pursue similar arrangements, potentially accelerating consolidation of North-South service networks and increasing competitive pressure on smaller operators. The key question for cargo owners surrounding any extension of alliances into new geographies will be whether it delivers a better-connected and more reliable North-South shipping network or simply a more concentrated one. Smaller shippers, particularly those reliant on secondary ports and less competitive trades, will worry that they could find themselves with fewer alternatives and less negotiating leverage. From the carrier viewpoint, ONE, and even Maersk, must be looking at the huge North-South network of market leader MSC and conclude that they need to cooperate to provide a competitive network (see Figure 1). Hapag-Lloyd, who currently partners Maersk on East-West routes in the Gemini Cooperation, would then consider that it also needs to find itself a North-South partner. Figure 1: Capacity by operator on major North-South routes, October 2026 Note: Based on capacity deployed on the following trades: Asia-Africa, Asia-Latin America, Asia-Oceania, Europe-Africa, Europe- Latin America, Europe-Oceania, North America-Africa, North America-Latin America, North America-Oceania, Africa-Latin America, Middle East/South Asia-Africa and Middle East/South Asia-Oceania. Conversely, clean product markets weakened across Western and Asian MR routes due to rising gasoline inventories and cooling regional buying, though LR2...
articles.body: Dirty freight stabilises as the market seeks a new equilibrium in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 28/11/2026 Dirty tanker rates rebounded across midsize segments this week, led by surging USG Aframax demand, while MEG VLCCs traded sideways amid looser regional tonnage. Conversely, clean product markets weakened across Western and Asian MR routes due to rising gasoline inventories and cooling regional buying, though LR2 rates firmed slightly on stronger Northeast Asian petrochemical margins. Market & Trading Calls MEG–China (TD3C): Slightly Bullish | VLCC rates levelled off at $29.62/bbl this week and are forecast to remain rangebound. Looser Gulf tonnage balances and lower Saudi loadings keep upward pressure capped. USG–China (TD22): Bullish | VLCC rates recouped losses, gaining $0.35/bbl to $17.43/bbl, and should remain supported. Tight tonnage and high GoO earnings continue to slow vessel replenishment in the region. WAF–UKC (TD20): Bullish | Suezmax rates jumped $0.60/bbl to $8.46/bbl and are expected to climb further. Strong VLCC and Aframax markets are pushing more cargoes onto Suezmaxes across the Atlantic. USG–UKC (TD25): Bullish | Aframax rates doubled to $17.51/bbl on record loadings and tight tonnage. However, increasing competition from larger Suezmaxes on transatlantic routes will likely temper further gains. Cross Med (TD19): Bullish | Aframax rates rose $1.22/bbl to $5.07/bbl and should sustain upward momentum. Record Red Sea/SUMED flows and firming Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline exports will lengthen regional cargo lists. MEG–Japan (TC1): Bearish | LR2 rates rose $0.83/bbl to $26.58/bbl but are expected to dip slightly next week. Weaker Asian LR demand offsets rising Northeast Asian cracker margins and Gulf security risks. UKC–USAC (TC2): Bearish | MR rates fell $0.27/bbl to $3.44/bbl and should drift lower next week. Rising US and European gasoline inventories continue to dampen transatlantic import demand. USG–UKC (TC14): Bearish | MR rates plunged 40% to $6.81/bbl, though losses should slow next week. Tightening Russian supply and reopening transatlantic arbitrage will eventually boost US Gulf diesel pull. Korea–Singapore (TC11): Bullish | MR rates dropped $1.28/bbl to $4.19/bbl but should level off and rise slightly. Low Chinese domestic diesel stocks argue against an expected flood of December export cargoes. VLCC MEG – China (TD3C) MEG to China VLCC rates levelled off over the reporting period, ending the week with a $0.04/bbl gain to $29.62/bbl. On the one hand, early November’s geopolitical optimism continues to dissipate, as highlighted by the ongoing targeting of commercial shipping in the MEG, as well as Houthi forces regaining control over the Red Sea coast of Yemen, followed by the announcement of yet another (unconfirmed) attack on Saudi Arabia’s Petroline. Inside the MEG, VLCC supply and demand balances have shown signs of stabilisation. Loadings have averaged 7.8 Mbd thus far in the month, with the largest m/m declines coming from Saudi Arabia. For comparison, at an estimated size of 103 vessels and an average round-trip duration of 24 days, the MEG shuttle VLCC fleet’s export capacity is estimated at approximately 8.3 Mbd per month, bringing MEG loadings below tonnage operating in the region for the first time since July. The future of this trend remains key, with Yanbu-to-East VLCC rates nearly 50% below MEG-to-East levels, potentially encouraging Saudi crude exports to Asia to shift towards lower-risk Red Sea ports, provided no further sabotage occurs. With current freight levels, largely reflecting this looser tonnage balance environment, the TD3c forecast remains rangebound. Broadly in line with MEG, GoO-to-China rates also traded sideways over the past week, shedding $0.03/bbl to $7.88/bbl. Regional rates continue to be pressured by VLCC employment in the EoS market, stabilising at 76% of the total fleet since mid-October. GoO loadings have also trended lower in November, with a drop in Meg loadings likely to eventually translate into reduced GoO StS in the medium term. VLCC MEG tonnage balance ratio (%) (10MA) vs TD3C ($/bbl) Source: Baltic Exchange, Kpler USG – China (TD22) USG to China VLCC rates recouped some of the early November’s losses, gaining $0.35/bbl to 17.43/bbl. On top of VLCCs practically exiting USG loadings thus far in November, wider West-East trades have come under pressure, currently tracking a low of 3 Mbd. The Brazil-to-East route remains the only consistently viable arbitrage, while WAF and WTI Midland-to-East opportunities have been circumstantial, with no sustained economic incentive to support continued flows. As such, support hinges on the supply side, where the small concentration of tonnage has seen the number of ballasters decrease. At the same time, GoO earnings continue to trade at a premium of circa $50k/day, decelerating the replenishment of tonnage in the region. We expect this trend to continue supporting USG VLCC rates until the earnings spread further narrows to incentivise more tonnage in the region. In the meantime, lack of VLCC tonnage is likely to pivot any West-East flows to midsizes, which thus far in November hold a market share of 52% of total flows. VLCC US Gulf tonnage balance ratio (%) (10MA) vs TD22 ($/bbl) Source: Baltic Exchange, Kpler Suezmax WAF – UKC (TD20) In line with our last week’s predictions, the rebound in the dirty rates accelerates as we move down to midsizes. In WAF, benchmark Suezmax rates to UKC increased by $0.60/bbl w/w, settling at $8.46/bbl. WAF remains the main region where strength in VLCCs is filtering down to Suezmaxes, primarily as Eastbound WAF cargoes shift to the more economical smaller vessels, with average VLCC-Suezmax rate spreads trading at parity so far in November. However, more recently we see Suezmaxes also benefiting from bottom-up support. Strong Aframax fundamentals, discussed below, have started pricing Suezmaxes into traditionally Aframax routes. Transatlantic USG-to-NWE trades have merged as the most evident example, where the $/bbl cost of Aframaxes currently dictates a premium of $9.30/bbl compared to Suezmaxes. As a result, going forward we expect Aframaxes to gradually lose their monopoly over intra-Atlantic trades, promoting Suezmax utilisation across the basin and thus rates. Suezmax WAF tonnage balance ratio (%) (10MA) vs TD20 ($/bbl) Source: Baltic Exchange, Kpler Aframax USG – UKC (TD25) USG to UKC Aframax rates led gains across the dirty segment over the past week, doubling in value to $17.51/bbl. As discussed in our last publication, the observed correction in TD25 rates largely contrasted with a fundamentally supported market, better reflecting the ripples of a weakening VLCC structure across the dirty complex. Indeed, with the exit of larger assets from the USG, Aframax loadings track a record 2.6 Mbd so far in November, even as the region’s overall loadings are trending lower. The recent decline in WTI, driven by inventory builds, alongside a relatively resilient Brent benchmark supported by the ongoing war premiums, has further allowed freight to move higher. High utilisation levels continue to bring tonnage availability down, further supporting assessments. However, we expect increasing penetration of larger assets in the transatlantic trades to start biting into the rates’ rally over the forecast. Aframax US Gulf tonnage balance ratio (%) (10MA) vs TD25 ($/bbl) Source: Baltic Exchange, Kpler Cross Med (TD19) Cross-MED Aframax rates also strengthened, although gains lagged significantly behind their transatlantic counterparts, rising by $1.22/bbl w/w to $5.07/bbl. While this increase partly reflects spillover strength from the Atlantic market, the route also benefits from firm underlying fundamentals. Red Sea and SUMED flows to Europe are currently running at a record 1.3 Mbd, with Aframaxes capturing the largest share at approximately 0.7 Mbd. Although Ceyhan loadings may have eased in November due to lower Kirkuk flows, some Iraqi volumes have been redirected to Syria, where SOMO has loaded its first Basrah cargo for trucking to Banias under an agreement signed in October. Looking ahead, Iraqi loadings at Ceyhan could soon exceed 500 kbd following SOMO’s resumption of flows through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline this week, lengthening regional cargo lists. Against this backdrop, we expect freight rates to sustain their upward momentum over the forecast period. Aframax Med tonnage balance ratio (%) (10MA) vs TD19 ($/bbl) Source: Baltic Exchange, Kpler LR2 MEG – Japan (TC1) MEG to Japan LR2 rates rose $0.83/bbl w/w to $26.58/bbl from $25.75/bbl, climbing steadily after a low of $25.66/bbl on 13 November. Rates have held up despite total Hormuz clearance of clean products falling this month. Asian pull is building with Northeast Asian steam-cracking margins at their highest since May 2023, and South Korean buyers will need further swing cargoes for end-December and early-January delivery as cracker turnarounds finish. Mediterranean naphtha also remains open to Asia on paper as clean freight softens. Offsetting this is weaker LR demand in Asia which have absorbed the bulk of the decline in regional flows, primarily from South Korea. An increase in West to East will add support to the wider LR market. Vessel attacks in the Gulf remain high, which is likely adding to the export weakness this month. Any easing of vessel attacks would let Middle Eastern naphtha and diesel exports recover towards pre-war levels, reducing the need for Western swing barrels. We expect rates to hold around current levels next week, dropping slightly. LR2 MEG tonnage balance ratio (%) (10MA) vs TC1 ($/bbl) . Source: Baltic Exchange, Kpler MR UKC – USAC (TC2) UKC to USAC MR rates fell $0.27/bbl w/w to $3.44/bbl from $3.71/bbl, reversing from a week high of $3.84/bbl on 16 November. The weakness reflects softening US demand for European gasoline. EIA data showed US gasoline stocks building by 5.2 mb in the week to 13 November, taking inventories 3% above the five-year average and to their highest since April, while diesel and jet stocks also rose. Northwest Europe gasoline exports are slowing, and falling retail prices have eased the urgency for the US to import. Europe is itself lengthening: ARA gasoline stocks are building rapidly, refinery maintenance is winding down, and export demand is weakening. West Africa offers some support, with flows rising in the last couple of weeks. Dangote exports are set to recover once partial RFCC maintenance wraps up this week, but this is unlikely to offset lost transatlantic demand. We expect rates to drift lower next week, finding support only if West African pull strengthens. MR UKC tonnage balance ratio (%) (10MA) vs TC2 ($/bbl) Source: Baltic Exchange, Kpler USG – UKC (TC14) USG to UKC MR rates dropped $4.61/bbl w/w to $6.81/bbl, a 40% decline from the $11.43/bbl open, with assessments falling in every session. The correction extends the slide across the Atlantic clean complex as LR freight in the West continues to soften and US product exports ease. Diesel fundamentals are firmer than the rate suggests. Repeated Ukrainian strikes on the Ust-Luga, Omsk, Volgograd, Ilsky and Salavat refineries are tightening Russian supply, and Russian exports are unlikely to meaningfully exceed 1 Mt next month, which should push Mediterranean and Latin American buyers back toward US Gulf Coast barrels. US diesel and jet exports are already up almost 60% y/y since March, the transatlantic diesel arbitrage into Europe has only just reopened, and record-low PADD 1 diesel stocks keep domestic demand for Gulf Coast supply firm. We expect the sharp decline to slow next week, with diesel pull limiting further losses. MR US Gulf tonnage balance ratio (%) (10MA) vs TC14 ($/bbl) Source: Baltic Exchange, Kpler Korea – Singapore (TC11) South Korea to Singapore MR rates fell $1.28/bbl w/w to $4.19/bbl from $5.47/bbl, with the decline accelerating on 19 November as the benchmark shed $0.71/bbl in a single session. Regional demand has cooled. Indonesian buying is expected to slow after a couple of strong weekly readings as stockpiling needs are met, while Chinese exports are tracking slightly lower m/m compared with expectations of higher planned allocations for November, which we believe will be deferred into December. Attention has turned to China’s December export programme. Refiners hold around 12 Mt of unused product export quota, and speculation that they will rush to use it has weighed on regional gasoil sentiment. However, reaching the 89% utilisation seen in 2024 and 2025 would take only about 7 Mt, and low domestic diesel stocks argue against a flood of cargoes. On the supply side, the ballast MR count has jumped this month following a shift in tonnage from West to East. We expect rates to level off next week before rising slightly as the market reaches a new balance. MR Eastern Asia tonnage balance ratio (%) (10MA) vs TC11 ($/bbl) Source: Baltic Exchange, Kpler Source: Kpler 2026-11-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Market & Trading Calls MEG–China (TD3C): Slightly Bullish | VLCC rates levelled off at $29.62/bbl this week and are forecast to remain rangebound.
Looser Gulf tonnage balances and lower Saudi loadings keep upward pressure capped.
USG–China (TD22): Bullish | VLCC rates recouped losses, gaining $0.35/bbl to $17.43/bbl, and should remain supported.

articles.body: GMS Week 48 – The Price of Standing Still in Weekly Demolition Reports 28/11/2026 Stability in the recycling market is becoming increasingly deceptive. While recycling indications remain unchanged across all four destinations, the commercial circumstances supporting them continue to evolve. Nowhere is this more apparent than in Bangladesh, where financially stretched recyclers are pursuing additional tonnage despite challenging downstream conditions. The overall market has barely moved, but maintaining that position is becoming a more complicated exercise for buyers. Dry freight has reversed last week’s retreat, with the Baltic Dry Index advancing from 2,901 on November 19 to 3,152 on Thursday, November 26. Capesizes strengthened to 5,100, Panamaxes improved to 2,273 and Supramaxes edged higher to 1,816. The recovery provides ageing vessels with renewed employment opportunities, offering little encouragement to recyclers awaiting a more consistent flow of candidates. Crude oil also reversed its recent downward trajectory. Brent traded around USD 97 per barrel on Friday morning, with WTI approaching USD 86, as renewed concerns over Middle Eastern energy supplies and shipping security supported prices. The recovery threatens to erode some of the recent relief in energy costs, while continuing uncertainty surrounding Gulf trading conditions may prolong employment opportunities for older tankers. Regional steel markets provided limited encouragement. Indian plate weakened considerably compared with last Friday, while Chinese quotations extended their decline. Bangladesh and Pakistan remained unchanged throughout the week. With downstream fundamentals offering little justification for stronger purchasing ideas, competition driven primarily by yard requirements deserves increasingly careful consideration. Bangladesh continues to display mixed buying sentiment, with financial commitments influencing the purchasing behaviour of certain recyclers. India encountered another regulatory hurdle following the European Parliament’s vote opposing the inclusion of two Alang facilities on the European List. Pakistan and Turkey maintained their measured approaches without any material change in underlying recycling sentiment. Waterfront activity continued across Alang and Chattogram, where several previously secured vessels progressed through delivery. Gadani’s position remained unchanged. Despite these movements, no new recycling sales were reported during the week, leaving the fresh sales pipeline considerably quieter than the operational waterfront. The market approaches December with familiar pricing but increasingly demanding commercial calculations. Stronger freight has restored confidence to owners, while recyclers must contend with uneven steel markets and the financial consequences of securing scarce tonnage. Standing still may appear the safest course, but for buyers carrying substantial financial commitments, even maintaining an existing position comes at a cost. articles.title: Frantic back-room haggling as climate deal for global shipping goes down to the wire
articles.summary: Over 120 governments are frantically trying to reach a compromise on the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), a historic climate agreement that would introduce the world’s first global carbon pricing, at the UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) in London. This week has been the technical negotiations (ISWG-GHG-23) on...
articles.body: Frantic back-room haggling as climate deal for global shipping goes down to the wire in International Shipping News 28/11/2026 Over 120 governments are frantically trying to reach a compromise on the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), a historic climate agreement that would introduce the world’s first global carbon pricing, at the UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) in London. This week has been the technical negotiations (ISWG-GHG-23) on 23-27 November. The IMO meets next week for decisive political negotiations (MEPC 85), on 30 November – 3 December, and (unlikely) the Extraordinary Session (MEPC E.2) on 4 December if the room is ready to adopt. Delegates met in the working group on Monday and in closed, informal discussions throughout the week, led by Japan and co-facilitated by Brazil, Canada, the European Commission, Ireland, Norway and China, to work towards consensus on the NZF’s key elements: the agreed limits to phase-out fossil fuels, clean energy and the carbon pricing revenues. The informal discussions are referenced in the outcome report of the meeting and are set to continue next week. Delegates observed that the majority of countries engaged constructively in the informal discussions to preserve the ambition in the NZF, with its opponents (US, Saudi Arabia and fellow petro states) looking increasingly isolated. Experts warn any further compromises that would water down the NZF’s elements would put at jeopardy the industry’s clean transition as well as vulnerable countries, and it would move the IMO even further away from achieving its own 2023 Revised Strategy commitments. Economic analysis by RMI + UCL says that the NZF is the best, most cost-effective policy tool amidst other alternatives to achieve the IMO’s own target: reaching net-zero by/around 2050 in an equitable way. The NZF remains on the table and it is the most mature policy package that can be adopted next week. Why this matters: Decisions at the IMO will decide the fate of ~5% of global oil demand represented by global shipping, responsible for around 3% of global emissions annually. Governments at the IMO committed to decarbonise the sector on a pathway consistent with the Paris Agreement’s safe temperature goals. Failing to agree on a global regulation for shipping would likely lead to a patchwork of national and regional regulation, which is already emerging in the EU, the UK and Africa, which would result in delay, uncertainty, and higher costs in the sector. Em Fenton (they/them), Senior Director of Climate Diplomacy at Opportunity Green, says: “The levels of ambition in the Net-Zero Framework have survived the first week of negotiations at the International Maritime Organization, but may not ultimately survive unscathed – with further compromise on the horizon. It is essential that Member States stand with courage in solidarity with the climate-vulnerable states whose very existence is threatened by a poor outcome at the IMO. Weakened ambition serves no one, it abandons developing countries and overlooks a genuine opportunity to deliver an economically-responsible maritime transition that’s fair for all. Member States must adopt the most ambitious outcome possible and accelerate a global maritime transition that leaves no country behind.” Lukas Leppert, President of the Clean Shipping Coalition, said: “After some IMO member states continued to launch attacks on climate ambition this week, the Marine Environment Protection Committee must turn things around. Next week, climate leaders within IMO member states have the singular opportunity of translating the IMO GHG Strategy into action – they must stand shoulder to shoulder, ignore distraction from false solutions and establish a global framework that meets shipping’s obligation to clean-up its climate warming emissions in a manner that leaves no state behind.” Angie Farrah-Thibault, Vice President, Global Transportation at Environmental Defense Fund, said: “The momentum at the IMO is real. While differences remain, Member States have been constructively building a blueprint for a maritime energy transition. Next week, they have the opportunity to turn that progress into action by adopting a binding global framework that gives industry the certainty to invest and deliver cleaner, more energy-secure and fairer shipping for everyone.” Fanny Devaux, Director, Shipping (Brussels, EU), T&E, said: “It is encouraging to see delegations engaging intensively, but dialogue must translate into concrete results next week. A deal is not an end in itself, it must be measured by its ability to deliver real emission cuts, not by how far governments compromise to protect fossil fuel interests.” Jamie Yates, Climate and Renewable Energy Manager, Pacific Environment, said: “We are heartened to see constructive engagement from all parties this week, as well as the continued development of an economic element as a critical component of the package. Next week will be the true test if climate ambition can survive compromise and whether any agreement will drive real change. Shipping needs a clear, strong framework to move towards net-zero and truly zero emissions. We urge member states to come refreshed to MEPC 85 ready to close the deal and move the industry off of fossil fuels and the sector towards a just and equitable transition.” Christiaan De Beukelaer, Senior Lecturer, University of Melbourne, said: “What the world needs is a proverbial horse-strength dose of antibiotics, to be able to withstand the climate crisis. This week, while most wanted to start administering a cure as soon as possible, petro-states, once again, tried to fool everyone into believing that a homeopathic dose is it. The NZF is nowhere near the ambition needed, but adopting anything weaker will simply lock in fossil LNG, thereby strengthening the disease all IMO member states have committed to eliminating.” Alisa Kreynes, Director of Ports and Shipping at C40 Cities, said, “The agreed Net-Zero Framework is an important basis for a just transition to cleaner shipping, but it is already a compromise. At the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) MEPC 85, Member States must preserve the elements agreed in April 2025, including the fuel intensity standard and greenhouse gas pricing mechanism, and avoid weakening them further. Especially after the disappointing outcomes of COP31, the shipping sector must maintain high ambition to stay within the 1.5°C limit in the Paris Agreement, while delivering fair support and tangible benefits to vulnerable countries and port communities.” Mike Robinson, CEO at 426 Maritime, said: “Electrification is no longer a promise, it is a product. More than 3,000 ships are already operating or on order with battery systems, built by over 100 manufacturers in 20 countries, and readiness levels have risen since 2023. What the industry needs now is a clear, durable signal from the IMO. Regulatory certainty is what turns proven technology into orders, and orders into scale.” Sources: Opportunity Green, Clean Shipping Coalition, Global Transportation at Environmental Defense Fund, T&E, Pacific Environment, University of Melbourne, C40 Cities and 426 Maritime 2026-11-28 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: This week has been the technical negotiations (ISWG-GHG-23) on 23-27 November.
The IMO meets next week for decisive political negotiations (MEPC 85), on 30 November – 3 December, and (unlikely) the Extraordinary Session (MEPC E.2) on 4 December if the room is ready to adopt.
The informal discussions are referenced in the outcome report of the meeting and are set to continue next week.

articles.body: Drewry: World Container Index Down 3% Last Week in International Shipping News 28/11/2026 For many years, World Container Index (WCI) has been the go-to, independent, global reference for index-linked contracts. If your organisation requires regional visibility/coverage beyond the eight trade lanes provided below, contact the team. Our detailed assessment for Thursday, 26 Nov 2026 • The Drewry World Container Index (WCI), the benchmark widely referenced by procurement teams, decreased 3% to $4,032 per 40ft container this week, driven by lower rates on the Transpacific trade route amid weak demand. • On the Transpacific trade route, rates continued their downtrend for the eighth consecutive week. Spot rates from Shanghai to New York decreased 7% to $7,615 per 40ft container, and those from Shanghai to Los Angeles fell 8% to $6,437 per 40ft container. Amid weak demand, carriers are reducing capacity through blank sailings. According to Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight, seven blank sailings have been announced for next week, compared with five this week. Despite these capacity reductions, Drewry expects freight rates to decrease further next week. • On the Asia-Europe/Med trade route, spot rates from Shanghai to Genoa increased 8% to $4,802 per 40ft container, while Shanghai to Rotterdam rates remained the same for the second consecutive week at $3,485 per 40ft container. Carriers are managing capacity through blank sailings. According to Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight, seven blank sailings (3 Asia-Europe, 4 Asia-Med) are announced for next week, higher than four (3 Asia-Europe, 1 Asia-Med) this week. As demand is expected to strengthen in December ahead of the new contract season and upcoming CNY, many carriers have announced PSS of $1,000–$1,500 per 40ft container on the Asia–Europe trade route, along with higher FAK rates of $4,500–$4,600 per 40ft container for Asia to North Europe and $6,400–$6,800 per 40ft container for Asia to Med, effective 1 December. As a result, Drewry expects rates to increase in the coming weeks. • The East–West container freight market is showing diverging trends, with rates increasing on Asia–Med while declining on Transpacific trade routes amid easing demand. Demand is expected to strengthen on Asia–Europe/Med trade routes in December. Meanwhile, European port congestion and continued geopolitical uncertainty in the Strait of Hormuz remain key concerns. • Suez Canal transits have been increasing as more carriers resume Red Sea routings; last week, 60 vessels transited the canal. The immediate risk of a watchmen strike at Los Angeles/Long Beach has eased following a tentative agreement. Shippers should expect continued freight rate volatility in December, driven by demand fluctuations, capacity management, port congestion, and geopolitical developments. articles.title: Maersk confirms order for twelve 24,000 TEU containerships

articles.body: Asia Dry Cargo Tankers Precious Shipping lines up five-ship buying spree Adis Ajdin November 28, 2026 0 178 1 minute read Thailand’s Precious Shipping is lining up the acquisition of five more vessels through a fresh series of joint ventures with Malaysia’s Emstraits Navigation and Singapore-based Lianson Fleet. The Khalid Hashim-led dry bulk owner said its wholly owned Singapore subsidiary, PSL Energy, had signed five joint venture agreements with the two companies, paving the way for five separate shipowning entities in Singapore. Each venture will acquire, own and operate one vessel, although ship types, acquisition prices and delivery schedules have yet to be disclosed. Precious and Lianson will each hold 49% of the new companies, with Emstraits taking the remaining 2%. The five ventures, provisionally named Nusantara Dahlia, Nusantara Hibiscus, Nusantara Iris, Nusantara Jasmines and Nusantara Lotus , are expected to be established within a month. The latest agreements build on an existing partnership between the three companies, which joined forces in March 2025 to establish Malaysia-based Nusantara Maritime, with Precious and Lianson each holding 45% and Emstraits controlling 10%. That venture has already taken Precious into the product tanker market. Earlier this year, the partners acquired the 2012-built, 51,758 dwt MR tanker High Tide for $28.45m. The vessel, since renamed Nusa Orchid , joined the Singapore-based Nusantara Orchid venture earlier this month. Precious has been widening its exposure beyond dry bulk while pressing ahead with the renewal of its core fleet. In September, the Bangkok-based owner ordered four 64,500 dwt ultramaxes at China’s Taizhou Sanfu Ship Engineering for a combined $141.8m, with deliveries stretching from 2030 into early 2031. By Yimou Lee and Greg Torode TAIPEI/HONG KONG, Nov 27 (Reuters) – China is staging a weeks-long amphibious landing drill in the province facing Taiwan, testing a new method to land troops ashore by linking civilian vessels into a makeshift floating bridge, satellite images and a research report showed. China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, despite Taipei’s rejection of Beijing’s sovereignty claims, and has never renounced the use of force to bring it under Chinese control. The exercise, in Dacheng Bay in China’s southeastern province of Fujian, was first spotted on November 1, according to satellite images and a report by geospatial data company ingeniSPACE reviewed by Reuters. “The People’s Liberation Army appeared to be rehearsing low-signature methods to provide logistical support to forces that could be involved in a first island chain invasion scenario,” said Jason Wang, the company’s chief operating officer. “Using civilian ships to enable bridging of heavy equipment and materiel from deeper waters creates additional locations they can use along the Taiwan coastline.” A senior security official briefed on the drill in Dacheng Bay, just 280 km (175 miles) from Taiwan’s main island, confirmed it was still in progress on Friday, but made no direct link to local elections set for the next day. VESSELS MANOEUVER AROUND BAY Analysis of the images from November 1 to 16 showed the vessels maneuvered around the bay, forming and dismantling a floating bridge about 800 m (2,600 ft) long, in activity also seen in images from commercial providers Vantor and Planet Labs. Eight civilian vessels participated, made up of four barges, two semi-submersible and two powered, along with four landing craft, as well as smaller support vessels and Chinese navy ships nearby, ingeniSPACE’s analysis and tracking data showed. No purpose-built bridging equipment was observed, suggesting China’s military may be honing its use of existing civilian maritime resources to improvise landing infrastructure in a combat scenario, ingeniSPACE said. The senior security official confirmed the report details. The drill was designed to “practice the swift seizure of small islands” and was “very targeted” at contingencies along the first island chain, the arc of islands stretching from Japan through Taiwan and the Philippines, the official said. It appeared to be part of this year’s “All-Military Strategic Exercise” by the Chinese military, and was routine but held later than in previous years, added the official, who sought anonymity, as the matter is a sensitive one. China’s defense ministry did not respond to a request for comment. Its training was “entirely legitimate and reasonable,” it said on Thursday, when asked about recent PLA drills in the region . Taiwan’s defense ministry said it was aware of Chinese military activity in Dacheng Bay, including the use of civilian vessels in exercises, and was weighing the implications for security in the Taiwan Strait and peace in the region. CHINA SEEN CONTINUOUSLY REFINING DRILLS China appears to be constantly refining coastal drills, said military attaches based in Asia, reflecting the immense task of attempting an amphibious landing across waters as wide as the Taiwan Strait. Rival militaries, including that of Taiwan, are known to scrutinize such efforts, they said. The drills are being held near Dongshan Island, visited by Chinese President Xi Jinping in 2024 and the site of a famous Cold War-era victory for the PLA. Here, in 1953, China’s military fought off an attempted invasion by Republic of China forces, which had fled to Taiwan in 1949 at the end of a civil war with Mao Zedong’s communists. While China ties have not been the focus of campaigning for Taiwan’s weekend local elections, Beijing has repeatedly denounced the ruling party’s candidate for Taipei mayor, whom it calls a “separatist.” JAMMING ACTIVITY SEEN AT DRILL LOCATION Jamming activity was observed in the area where the drill was held, ingeniSPACE’s Wang added, citing a blurry synthetic aperture radar image obtained by the company. Taiwan has previously disclosed Chinese amphibious landing drills in Dacheng Bay in 2023 and 2024 involving roll-on/roll-off freighters. Both took place in September. Reuters documented similar drills off the southern coast of Guangdong in August last year, showing China was rehearsing the use of civilian shipping to supplement any Taiwan operation. The drill showed China’s military was increasingly focused on island-group operations, added the senior security official, but cautioned against overstating its battlefield value. “There is still some distance between innovation and fantasy,” the official said, adding that barges would be “live targets” in wartime. REUTERS/Lucila Sigal By Katharine Gemmell Nov 27, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Guinea’s giant Simandou iron ore project, which began stepping up production this year, has exported its first cargo to a European customer, according to Kpler. The shipment is a milestone that marks the first cargo to a country outside China, a major backer of the mine and home to the world’s biggest steel industry. A vessel named Tower Point left the project’s Morebaya port laden with 79,081 tons of Simandou Fines on Nov. 23, bound for Dunkirk in France for arrival in early December, according to the data and analytics firm. European steelmaker ArcelorMittal SA has a plant in Dunkirk. Kpler’s data shows the cargo was shipped by Simfer, a venture between Rio Tinto Group and Aluminum Corp. of China that owns two of Simandou’s four blocks. The consortium that owns the other blocks includes China Baowu Steel Group Corp., the country’s top steel mill, alongside a Singaporean firm. Simandou’s high-grade ore, which is best suited for low-emissions steelmaking, has been primarily earmarked for China. Rio Tinto and ArcelorMittal declined to comment. Simandou has steadily ramped up this year toward an annual capacity target of 120 million tons. Monthly exports from Guinea surpassed 5 million tons for the first time in October, with 22 million tons shipped so far in 2026, according to the Baltic and International Maritime Council, a shipping association. ArcelorMittal is the world’s No. 2 steel mill by output after Baowu and operates its own mines across the globe. articles.title: Building a Culture of Safety: Leadership, Accountability, and Workforce Commitment
articles.summary: In the ship repair industry, safety is more than a regulatory requirement or a box to check. It is a fundamental part of successful operations and a responsibility that must be reinforced...

Join the leading maritime news network In the ship repair industry, safety is more than a regulatory requirement or a box to check. It is a fundamental part of successful operations and a responsibility that must be reinforced throughout every level of an organization. Shipyards are dynamic working environments where employees perform complex tasks involving heavy equipment, welding, fabrication, confined spaces, elevated work areas, and simultaneous operations across multiple vessels. Each project presents unique challenges, and work conditions can change throughout the day. Maintaining a safe working environment requires more than written procedures and compliance programs. It requires visible leadership, consistent accountability, and a commitment shared by every employee. At Alabama Shipyard, employee safety is a core operational priority and an essential part of the company’s approach to workforce management and operational excellence. Safety Starts with Senior Management A strong safety culture begins with ownership at the senior management level. Leadership establishes the expectations, accountability, and organizational support necessary to make safety an integral part of daily operations. Without visible commitment and consistent support from senior management, employees may lack the confidence to raise concerns, challenge unsafe conditions, or exercise Stop Work Authority when necessary. In a shipyard environment, where project requirements, work conditions, and operational priorities can change throughout the day, management must demonstrate that safety takes precedence in every operational decision. This commitment extends beyond establishing policies and procedures. It requires providing the resources necessary to support safe operations, reinforcing expectations through consistent communication, and holding all levels of the organization accountable. Equally important is creating an environment where employees know they have the full support of management when exercising Stop Work Authority. Employees must feel empowered to identify hazards, communicate concerns, and stop work when conditions are unsafe without fear of reprisal or pressure to prioritize production over safety. No schedule, production target, or project requirement should take precedence over employee safety. This expectation must be consistently demonstrated through leadership actions and reinforced throughout the organization. Ultimately, safety cannot be delegated to a single department or individual. It requires ownership from senior leadership, accountability from supervisors, and active participation from the entire workforce. Beyond Compliance: Making Safety Part of Daily Operations Regulatory compliance provides the foundation for workplace safety, but an effective safety program must extend beyond meeting minimum requirements. In ship repair, maintaining safe operations requires continuous planning, communication, and coordination among shipyard personnel, vessel crews, subcontractors, and customers. Pre-job safety meetings, employee training, routine inspections, and job hazard assessments are essential components of identifying and addressing potential risks before work begins. These practices are particularly important when managing simultaneous operations across multiple trades, coordinating hot work and confined-space activities, or adapting to changing vessel and worksite conditions. Effective communication and coordination help ensure that employees understand the hazards associated with their work and the precautions necessary to perform it safely. Safety considerations must remain an active part of project planning and execution, rather than being addressed only when an issue arises. A well-established safety culture benefits more than the workforce. Effective safety practices also support operational consistency, minimize disruptions, strengthen customer confidence, and contribute to the successful execution of complex vessel repair and maintenance projects. Recognizing a Continued Commitment to Safety Alabama Shipyard has established a strong record of safety performance and industry leadership, earning the Shipbuilders Council of America (SCA) Excellence in Safety Award for five consecutive years, most recently in 2026, and recognition as one of AEU’s Safety Award recipients in 2022. These recognitions reflect more than industry achievement; they represent Alabama Shipyard’s ongoing commitment to protecting its workforce and making safety an integral part of every operation. Through leadership commitment, employee accountability, and continuous improvement, Alabama Shipyard strives to maintain a work environment where safety is a shared organizational responsibility. While industry recognition is a significant accomplishment, the true measure of a successful safety program is the consistency with which safety expectations are upheld in daily operations. Senior management must establish clear expectations, demonstrate accountability, and provide the resources necessary to support safe operations. Equally important, employees must have the confidence and support to identify hazards, raise concerns, and exercise Stop Work Authority when necessary. Ultimately, safety is measured not by awards or written policies, but by the decisions made and actions taken every day. It requires visible leadership, active workforce participation, and accountability at every level of the organization. Alabama Shipyard remains committed to fostering a culture where every employee is empowered and expected to take ownership of safety, look out for coworkers, and ensure that everyone returns home safely at the end of each shift. Investing in People and the Future of the Maritime Industry The future of the American maritime industry depends heavily on its ability to attract, develop, and retain a skilled workforce. As demand for domestic ship repair and maintenance continues to evolve, maintaining a qualified and safety-conscious workforce will remain a priority for shipyards throughout the country. Workforce development extends beyond recruiting and hiring. Providing employees with the training, resources, and support necessary to perform their jobs safely and effectively is essential to building a sustainable workforce. Continued training helps employees adapt to evolving technologies, operational requirements, and industry standards, while experienced employees play an important role in transferring knowledge and reinforcing established safety practices. Equally important is creating a workplace where employees feel valued, supported, and confident that their safety is a priority. Organizations that invest in employee development and maintain a strong commitment to workplace safety are better positioned to build an engaged and capable workforce. At Alabama Shipyard, the workforce remains one of the company’s most important assets. Protecting employees, supporting their professional development, and reinforcing a culture of accountability are essential to maintaining the skilled workforce needed to support the maritime industry’s future. A Commitment That Never Stops Operational excellence is not achieved through a single initiative, policy, or industry award. It is built through consistent leadership, accountability, and a shared commitment to maintaining the highest standards of safety. For Alabama Shipyard, protecting its workforce is an ongoing responsibility that extends across every department, project, and level of the organization. It requires senior management to lead by example, supervisors to reinforce expectations, and employees to remain engaged and accountable for their own safety and the safety of those around them. As the American maritime industry continues to grow and evolve, the importance of protecting the people who maintain, repair, and sustain the nation’s fleet remains constant. Because ultimately, successful shipyard operations begin with strong leadership, a committed workforce, and a culture where safety always comes first. Established in 2018, the shipyard operates one of the largest floating dry docks in the Gulf region and offers deepwater access and extensive waterfront infrastructure to support large-scale and complex vessel maintenance, repair, overhaul, and conversion (MROC) projects. articles.title: MISC Profit Surges 78%, LNG Fleet Expansion Accelerates
articles.summary: Strong petroleum shipping markets, offshore construction activity and fleet renewal lifted MISC's third-quarter results, although the Malaysian shipping group sees contrasting prospects for tanker and LNG carrier markets.Malaysia's MISC Berhad…
articles.body: MISC Profit Surges 78%, LNG Fleet Expansion Accelerates Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 27, 2026 Datuk Zahid Osman, MISC President and Group CEO. Image courtesy MISC Strong petroleum shipping markets, offshore construction activity and fleet renewal lifted MISC's third-quarter results, although the Malaysian shipping group sees contrasting prospects for tanker and LNG carrier markets. Malaysia's MISC Berhad reported a 77.5% increase in third-quarter net profit attributable to shareholders, as elevated tanker freight rates, increased vessel earning days and progress on offshore construction projects drove a sharp improvement in earnings. For the quarter ended September 30, 2026, MISC recorded revenue of RM3.92 billion ($3.92 billion in Malaysian ringgit terms), up 40.2% from RM2.80 billion a year earlier. Operating profit climbed 64.9% to RM1.08 billion, while profit attributable to shareholders reached RM961.8 million, compared with RM541.8 million in the corresponding 2025 quarter. For the first nine months, revenue increased 39.3% to RM11.61 billion, while attributable profit rose 66.9% to RM2.86 billion. Operating cash flow increased 28.2% to RM4.82 billion. The principal earnings driver was MISC's Petroleum & Products shipping business, which benefited from higher freight rates and increased earning days. Geopolitical disruptions in the Middle East and Red Sea have complicated crude oil transportation, extending voyages and reducing effective tanker availability. MISC expects these conditions, combined with increasing cargo volumes, to continue supporting tanker demand and freight rates in the near term. "Our Petroleum business continued to leverage its commercial agility to capture opportunities presented by elevated tanker rates," said Datuk Zahid Osman, MISC President and Group CEO. However, the outlook is considerably different for LNG shipping, where an expanding global carrier fleet is outpacing available cargoes. MISC expects LNG carrier spot charter rates to remain under pressure, compounded by Middle East LNG supply disruptions. Longer-term charter rates are expected to remain more resilient as additional liquefaction capacity enters service and charterers seek greater certainty over vessel availability. That distinction is shaping MISC's fleet development strategy. During the third quarter, MISC took delivery of two LNG carriers serving QatarEnergy through a consortium partnership. It also secured a 10-year charter from Malaysia LNG Sdn Bhd for a newbuild 18,700-cu.m. LNG carrier scheduled to begin employment in 2028. In October, MISC secured contracts for five additional newbuild LNG carriers from PETRONAS LNG Ltd, each backed by a 20-year charter commencing in 2030. The contracts expand MISC's portfolio of long-term contracted tonnage while supporting the replacement of older vessels. Fleet rationalization remains another priority. MISC reported lower revenue in its Gas Assets & Solutions business during the first nine months, reflecting vessel disposals, layups, reduced earning days and lower charter rates. Accelerated depreciation on older vessels also weighed on operating profit. In petroleum shipping, MISC intends to continue introducing dual-fuel vessels, expand contracted employment and optimize fleet deployment to capitalize on favorable tanker markets. Beyond shipping, offshore construction contributed to the improved results. Revenue benefited from increased construction progress on a floating storage and offloading unit and a floating production unit, while marine and heavy engineering projects advanced into higher-value construction phases. Looking ahead, MISC sees continued opportunities for floating production, storage and offloading projects in Asia, South America and Africa, supported by upstream oil and gas investment. The group has also signed a collaboration agreement with MHB and Wison New Energies covering offshore production facilities, floating LNG, vessel newbuilding and conversions, and carbon capture and storage. articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables Netherlands opens 2GW offshore wind tender Bojan Lepic November 27, 2026 0 234 1 minute read Alpha Ventus Alpha Ventus The Netherlands has launched tenders for two offshore wind farms with a combined generating capacity of 2GW, backed by a maximum subsidy budget of nearly €9.5bn ($10.43bn). The Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO) opened applications on Thursday for development permits for the IJmuiden Ver Gamma-A and Gamma-B offshore wind sites. Each site can accommodate a 1GW offshore wind farm, with applications open until December 10. The maximum subsidy budget has been set at €4.758bn for Gamma-A and €4.698bn for Gamma-B, with maximum tender prices of €117 and €116 per MWh, respectively. If no such bids are received, applications seeking financial support will be ranked according to the lowest subsidy requested. The Dutch government increased the maximum combined subsidy budget from around €7.9bn earlier this year following concerns over rising offshore wind development costs and the planned introduction of charges for using the high-voltage electricity grid. The tender is being conducted under a temporary offshore wind support mechanism introduced ahead of the Netherlands’ planned adoption of a contract-for-difference system from mid-2027. The two wind farms will share offshore grid infrastructure developed by Dutch transmission system operator TenneT, including a 2GW direct current connection to the mainland. The Gamma sites form part of the wider IJmuiden Ver offshore wind zone, which is expected to accommodate around 6GW of generating capacity. RVO expects to award the development permits during the first quarter of 2027, with both wind farms scheduled to enter commercial operation in 2032. Re-entering the market will require Japanese yards to rebuild specialist engineering expertise, secure access to modern cargo containment technology and re-establish supply chains for cryogenic equipment. The proposed cooperation comes as Tokyo looks to double Japan’s annual shipbuilding output to 18m gt by 2035, reversing decades of declining global market share. LNG carriers represent one of the highest-value segments of the commercial shipbuilding market, with newbuilding prices remaining above $200m. Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS By Weilun Soon Nov 26, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has risen this month, according to data from Vortexa , even as attacks on vessels in the contested waterway have increased. The number of ships carrying crude, fuels and liquefied natural gas stayed above 26, on a seven-day moving average basis, this month through Nov. 19, the figures show. That compares with October, when transits were below 25 on at least two-thirds of the days. The Vortexa data also show the amount of very large crude carriers and Suezmaxes crossing the strait has decreased slightly, while the number of smaller vessels has risen. This comes as oil-product tankers, which are smaller than crude carriers, are increasingly being converted to transport oil. The danger of shipping energy through Hormuz has increased in recent weeks. Iran has launched a wave of attacks on tankers, while widening the scope of vessels it says shouldn’t be transiting the waterway to include tugboats . Meanwhile, the cost to shuttle oil through the strait and additional insurance fees have also risen to near war-time highs, a reflection of the risks shipowners are taking to make the passage. The numbers, however, may not capture all of the vessels moving through Hormuz. Signal interference, spoofing and dark transits may affect real-time monitoring of data and the tally may be revised when more information becomes available, Vortexa said. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: At least one crew member aboard a ship carrying diesel has died after the vessel capsized and partially sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza on Thursday, regional authorities said, adding there were no signs of pollution so far.

Spanish Transport Ministry/via Reuters TV/Handout via REUTERS THIS IMAGE HAS BEEN SUPPLIED BY A THIRD PARTY MADRID, Nov 26 (Reuters) – At least one crew member aboard a ship carrying diesel has died after the vessel capsized and partially sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza on Thursday, regional authorities said, adding there were no signs of pollution so far. The Malta-flagged chemical tanker Med Emre was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona and may have been carrying up to 7,000 metric tons of diesel when it keeled over about 30 nautical miles (56 km) off Ibiza’s northwestern coast, the Balearic Islands’ interior department said. Emergency services said all 17 crew members were rescued, but one died after being taken directly to Ibiza’s Can Misses hospital. Six others were brought to Ibiza airport and taken to two hospitals with light injuries, primarily hypothermia. Of the remaining crew, five were taken to Valencia and five remained in good condition aboard a rescue vessel, they added. Pablo Garriz, the Balearic Islands’ regional head of emergencies, said the crew included Turkish and Indian nationals, but he could not yet confirm the nationality of the deceased. The tanker remained partially submerged with its keel protruding above the surface, Garriz told reporters, despite initial indications that it had sunk completely. “The positive news is that the vessel is not on the seabed but remains semi-submerged at the surface, which allows salvage and containment operations,” he said, adding there was currently no impact on Balearic waters or coastline and no evidence of a significant spill, although small sheens had been observed. Technical experts were assessing the vessel’s stability before deciding on salvage and cargo-recovery operations, he added. Spain’s maritime rescue service sent an aircraft and a vessel specialized in oil-spill response, the Clara Campoamor, to survey the area. Three helicopters took part in the rescue, along with nearby merchant vessels. Spain’s merchant marine authority activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest. The waters surrounding Ibiza are a habitat for sea turtles, dolphins and the Balearic shearwater, one of Europe’s most threatened seabirds. The area is also home to extensive meadows of Posidonia oceanica seagrass, which plays a vital role in supporting marine biodiversity. Spain’s worst maritime environmental disaster occurred in 2002, when the Bahamas-flagged tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region, spilling tens of thousands of tons of heavy fuel oil and fouling hundreds of beaches in Spain and France.
